entities.name: John I of Lubin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John I, Duke of Lüben (Lubin), a member of the Silesian Piast dynasty, governed fragmented territories within the Bohemian Crown from 1441 until his death in 1453. His reign, primarily centered on the duchies of Lubin and Haynau (Chojnów), represents a critical juncture in the late medieval political landscape of Silesia, characterized by the gradual absorption of independent Piast duchies into larger regional powers. As the last direct male descendant of the Lubin-Haynau branch, his demise without issue precipitated a significant territorial shift, influencing the balance of power between the local Piast dukes and the Bohemian Crown.

Upon the death of his father, Duke Louis III of Oława, in 1441, John I initially co-ruled the duchies of Lubin and Haynau with his younger brother, Henry X. Their mother, Margareta of Opava, served as regent during their minority, navigating the complex political currents of the region. From 1449 to 1450, John I and Henry X also jointly administered the strategically important duchies of Brieg (Brzeg) and Goldberg (Złotoryja). Following Henry X's death in 1452, John I became the sole ruler of Lubin and Haynau, consolidating his direct control over these hereditary lands, albeit for a short period.

The most profound legacy of John I's rule was its abrupt termination. His death in 1453, without any surviving legitimate heirs, directly triggered the reversion of the Duchies of Lubin and Haynau to the suzerainty of the Bohemian Crown. This event effectively extinguished the Lubin-Haynau line of the Silesian Piasts, marking a crucial step in the systemic process of Silesian territories being absorbed by the larger political entities that would shape Central Europe for centuries to come. The lands were subsequently granted to Frederick I of Liegnitz (Legnica), a cousin from another Piast branch, under Bohemian suzerainty.
